 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you do?

Package: golang.org/x/tools/present
File: present/parse.go (parseSections, Section.HTMLAttributes)
Tested: v0.49.0

Rendered a .slide file whose .background directive carries a crafted argument:

 .background x")onmouseover=alert(document.domain)//

The .background handling in parseSections builds an inline style from this argument and the result is emitted as an HTML attribute.

Filed as a hardening issue, consistent with golang/go#80859.

### What did you see happen?

The argument is concatenated into a style string without escaping:

 section.Styles = append(section.Styles,
 "background-image: url('"+args[1]+"')")

Section.HTMLAttributes() then emits it as:

 fmt.Sprintf(`style=%q`, strings.Join(s.Styles, " "))

and returns the value as template.HTMLAttr, which tells html/template the attribute is already safe and must not be escaped.

The %q verb applies Go string escaping (it turns " into \"). HTML parsers do not treat \ as an escape character, so the " still closes the style attribute.
The attacker-controlled argument therefore breaks out of the attribute and injects additional attributes/markup — e.g. an onmouseover handler. It fires on mouseover, with no click required.

### What did you expect to see?

The .background argument should be validated before it is used, the same way the parser already rejects other malformed directives. Specifically:

- reject characters that could terminate the url(...) context or the style
 attribute (quotes, parentheses, backslash, angle brackets), and
- restrict the URL scheme to an allowlist (http, https, or a relative path).

Invalid input should return a parse error instead of producing an attribute that escapes html/template's protections.

Happy to send a CL.

### What did you do?

I used httputil.ReverseProxy with ModifyResponse to replace the response body and update its length.

The documentation for http.Response says:

> When Header values are duplicated by other fields in this struct (e.g., ContentLength, TransferEncoding, Trailer), the field values are authoritative.

Based on this, I wrote the following program:

 [CODE_BLOCK] package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "io"
 "net/http"
 "net/http/httptest"
 "net/http/httputil"
 "net/url"
 "strings"
)

func main() {
 backend := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, _ *http.Request) {
 w.Header().Set("Content-Length", "5")
 io.WriteString(w, "hello")
 }))
 defer backend.Close()

 target, _ := url.Parse(backend.URL)
 proxy := httputil.NewSingleHostReverseProxy(target)

 proxy.ModifyResponse = func(res *http.Response) error {
 res.Body.Close()
 res.Body = io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader("x"))
 res.ContentLength = 1
 return nil
 }

 rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
 req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/", nil)

 proxy.ServeHTTP(rec, req)

 fmt.Println(rec.Result().Header.Get("Content-Length"))
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen?

The program prints:

5

`ReverseProxy` preserves the original `Content-Length: 5` value from Response.Header, even though `ModifyResponse` changes:

`res.ContentLength = 1`

and replaces the response body with a 1-byte body.

### What did you expect to see?

Based on the documented semantics of `http.Response`, I expected the resulting response to have:

`Content-Length: 1`

I'm not sure whether the current `ReverseProxy` behavior is intentional.

Title: cmd/go: `go work sync` writes go.sum files missing the go.mod hashes of the versions it upgrades to

Body: ### Go version

`go version go1.27.0 linux/amd64` (also reproduces on go1.25.0 and on tip)

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

 [CODE_BLOCK] GO111MODULE=''
GOARCH='amd64'
GOOS='linux'
GOPROXY='[URL]
GOSUMDB='sum.golang.org'
GOTOOLCHAIN='go1.27.0'

 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you do?

A workspace with two modules that both import `golang.org/x/text/language`, at different versions, each with a tidy `go.sum`:

 [CODE_BLOCK] -- go.work --
go 1.21

use (
 ./a
 ./b
)
-- a/go.mod --
module example.com/a

go 1.21

require golang.org/x/text v0.41.0
-- a/a.go --
package a

import _ "golang.org/x/text/language"
-- a/go.sum --
golang.org/x/text v0.41.0 h1:vz/seA0lnX87Othu2f/0L24RcgrXD9/YFTSuGjj3rH8=
golang.org/x/text v0.41.0/go.mod h1:jvf1O8ajNzZqhSrQBPbutR/EB83Cc0CFrezNQIwbb5M=
-- b/go.mod --
module example.com/b

go 1.21

require golang.org/x/text v0.40.0
-- b/b.go --
package b

import _ "golang.org/x/text/language"
-- b/go.sum --
golang.org/x/text v0.40.0 h1:Ub2Z6/xjgF1WrYQz2nuITOEegKFtiIy+rieRJ5lHZKs=
golang.org/x/text v0.40.0/go.mod h1:hpnzDAfGV753zIKo+wk3u1bVKCGPbrnF7+7LBF/UHVY=
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Then:

 [CODE_BLOCK] go work sync
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen?

`go work sync` upgraded `b` to `golang.org/x/text v0.41.0` and rewrote `b/go.sum` with the module hash but without the `go.mod` hash:

 [CODE_BLOCK] $ cat b/go.sum
golang.org/x/text v0.41.0 h1:vz/seA0lnX87Othu2f/0L24RcgrXD9/YFTSuGjj3rH8=
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

So `b` no longer builds on its own, outside the workspace:

 [CODE_BLOCK] $ GOWORK=off go -C b build ./...
b.go:3:8: golang.org/x/text@v0.41.0: missing go.sum entry for go.mod file; to add it:
 go mod download golang.org/x/text
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

and `go mod tidy` puts the missing line back:

 [CODE_BLOCK] $ GOWORK=off go -C b mod tidy
$ cat b/go.sum
golang.org/x/text v0.41.0 h1:vz/seA0lnX87Othu2f/0L24RcgrXD9/YFTSuGjj3rH8=
golang.org/x/text v0.41.0/go.mod h1:jvf1O8ajNzZqhSrQBPbutR/EB83Cc0CFrezNQIwbb5M=
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Nothing in workspace mode notices, because in workspace mode the checksums are looked up in the collective set of the workspace modules' `go.sum` files, and `a/go.sum` has the missing line. Repeated `go work sync` runs stay clean; the breakage only shows up when the module is built or tidied on its own, e.g. by CI that builds one module of a multi-module repository.

Here is the same thing as a hermetic `cmd/go` testscript, using the test module proxy (both `grep` lines are the bug; the `go build` at the end fails today):

 [CODE_BLOCK] # testdata/script/work_sync_gosum_gomod.txt
go -C a mod tidy
go -C b mod tidy
grep '^rsc.io/quote v1.0.0/go.mod ' b/go.sum

 [CODE_BLOCK] y0 := y // save y

 [/CODE_BLOCK]

Title: x/website/cmd/screentest: reject negative retrypixels values

Body: Both the global -retrypixels flag and the per-test retrypixels directive accept negative values.

The configured value is later compared as follows:

 [CODE_BLOCK] if result.DiffPixelsCount > uint64(tc.retryPixels) {
 break
 }
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

For example, uint64(-1) is math.MaxUint64. As a result, every non-equal comparison between same-sized images is considered retryable. Screentest then consumes all three attempts, even when the difference is large.

For HTTP(S) inputs this can cause repeated browser screenshot captures.

For file or GCS inputs it causes repeated image reads. The final comparison still reports a failure if all attempts remain different, but the invalid
configuration is not detected and the output contains:

 `difference is <= -1 pixels`

Negative values should be rejected for both the global flag and the per-test directive.

Title: runtime: support TLS slot indices over 64 on Windows

Body: Since go 1.20, the Go runtime allocates the TLS slot in the TEB TlsSlots instead of using the TEB arbitrary pointer. See CL 431775 for more context.

The problem is that the static TEB TlsSlots array only has capacity for 64 indices, when more slots are required TlsAlloc allocates them on a heap-allocated array. TlsGetValue abstracts this implementation detail, but we don't use `TlsGetValue` and our logic to retrieve the TLS value does not currently support retrieving the value from TlsSlots or the heap depending on the index.

For now I've submitted CL 486816 to fallback to the old behavior (TEB arbitrary pointer) in case the TLS index is higher than 64. This solution is temporal, as we should rely on the TEB arbitrary pointer.

This issue should track the effort (small or big, still don't know) to implement a solution that supported TLS indices higher than 64.

Title: math: Log2 has a large relative error near 1

Body: ### Go version

go version go1.27.0 darwin/arm64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

CC='cc'

GOTOOLCHAIN='auto'
GOVERSION='go1.27.0'
GOWORK=''
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you do?

 [CODE_BLOCK] package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "math"
)

func main() {
 x := math.Nextafter(1, 2)

 fmt.Println(math.Log2(x))
 fmt.Println(math.Log1p(x-1) * (1 / math.Ln2))
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen?

On go.dev/play (linux/amd64):

 [CODE_BLOCK] 3.3306690738754696e-16
3.203426503814917e-16
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

On darwin/arm64 with Go 1.27.0:

 [CODE_BLOCK] 3.6790862436379807e-16
3.203426503814917e-16
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you expect to see?

The correctly rounded value of `log2(1 + 2^-52)` is `3.203426503814917e-16`,
which is what the second line returns on both platforms. `math.Log2` returns
`3.3306690738754696e-16` on amd64 — a relative error of 4.0%, about `2.6e14` ulp —
and `3.6790862436379807e-16` on arm64 — 14.9%, about `9.6e14` ulp.

Go does not guarantee correctly rounded or bit-identical cross-platform results.
Here, however, the errors are 4–15%, and the two platforms differ from each other
by about 10% of the correct value.

### Cause

`src/math/log10.go`:

 [CODE_BLOCK] func log2(x float64) float64 {
 frac, exp := Frexp(x)
 // Make sure exact powers of two give an exact answer.
 // Don't depend on Log(0.5)*(1/Ln2)+exp being exactly exp-1.
 if frac == 0.5 {
 return float64(exp - 1)
 }
 return Log(frac)*(1/Ln2) + float64(exp)
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

For `x = 1 + 2^-52`, `Frexp` returns `frac = 0.5000000000000001` and
`exp = 1`. When evaluated separately, the product rounds to
`-0.9999999999999997`. Adding `1` cancels almost all significant digits.

The final multiply and add are fused into an `FMADDD` on arm64. On amd64 the
product is rounded before the addition. Both behaviors are allowed by the Go
specification. `math.FMA(Log(frac), 1/Ln2, float64(exp))` reproduces the arm64
result; rounding the product first reproduces the amd64 result. The cancellation
makes this normally small difference visible.

### Suggested fix

 [CODE_BLOCK] func log2(x float64) float64 {
 frac, exp := Frexp(x)
 // Make sure exact powers of two give an exact answer.
 // Don't depend on Log(0.5)*(1/Ln2)+exp being exactly exp-1.
 if frac == 0.5 {
 return float64(exp - 1)
 }
 // Avoid cancellation near 1. x-1 is exact in [0.5, 2).
 if exp == 0 || exp == 1 {
 return Log1p(x-1) * (1 / Ln2)
 }
 return Log(frac)*(1/Ln2) + float64(exp)
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

I tested 13,442 values across the float64 range, with extra coverage around 1,
on darwin/arm64. The oracle was cross-checked at 40, 60, and 120 decimal digits.
The table below is therefore the arm64 column; I have not run the sweep on amd64
hardware, only the single value shown above.

| | current | proposed |
|---|---:|---:|
| worst error | `9.6e14` ulp | 1.31 ulp |
| points above 1 ulp | 1,475 | 64 |

All 1,475 current failures were within `|x-1| ≤ 0.25`. Powers of two remain
exact. Results for ±0, ±Inf, NaN, negative values, and subnormals are unchanged.

### Cost

`go test math` passes with this change on go1.27.0, darwin/arm64.

Benchmarks on an M3, four runs of 400 ms over 1,024 arguments:

| | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| arguments spread over `[0.25, 7500]` | 5.41 ns/op | 5.60–6.04 ns/op |
| arguments in `[1, 1.001]` (the new branch) | 5.47 ns/op | 4.55 ns/op |

The mixed-input benchmark is 4–12% slower. The near-1 benchmark is 17% faster.
`log2` is not inlinable before or after the change.

I can send a CL with tests if this approach looks reasonable.

Title: x/image/vector: rasterizer shifts alpha mask and is slow when target is offset and small relative image size

Body: Please answer these questions before submitting your issue. Thanks!

### What version of Go are you using (`go version`)?
1.10.2

### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?
Yes

### What operating system and processor architecture are you using (`go env`)?
linux/amd64

### What did you do?
In the golang.org/x/image/vector.go there is this function: 

```func (z *Rasterizer) Draw(dst draw.Image, r image.Rectangle, src image.Image, sp image.Point)```
r is the target rectangle for rendering the image. When r is a smaller rectangle than the bounds of the destination image dst, and offset into the middle of dst, two problems emerge:

First, the alpha mask, which is the whole point of the Draw command shifts with the target rectangle rather than staying fixed to the upper left corner of the image. I believe this should not be the default behavior. It is not consistent with other rasterizers, such as the free type rasterizer. If the mask shifts with the target and you are rendering a path using, say, Bezier curves, and want to draw that path onto an image, you must either determine before hand the exact boundaries of the path and shift the coordinates accordingly, because as it is, a target drawn somewhere in the middle of an image will always draw the mask relative to the upper left corner of the target rectangle. Having to determine the boundaries before hand requires flattening the curves and either storing the resulting line segments or repeating the process when actually rendering the alpha mask. It is much simpler to keep the alpha mask fixed to the upper left corner of the image boundary rather than move with the target rectangle.

Second, no matter how big the target rectangle is relative to the entire image, the "accumulate step" traverses the entire image, which is inefficient when the target is a small fraction of the image. 

I have created a modified version of the rasterizer here: [URL]

In the vector_test.go file are modified versions of the TestBasicPathDstAlpha and TestBasicPathDstRGBA test functions. These are changed to test for fixing the alpha mask to the image and not shifting with the target. They will fail with the current version of vector.go, but not the forked version. 

There are also a series of benchmarks showing the improved performance when the target is small relative the destination image. This is what the benchmark output looks like:
```
BenchmarkDrawPathBounds1000-16 30 44412739 ns/op
BenchmarkDrawImageBounds1000-16 20 53485352 ns/op
BenchmarkDrawPathBounds100-16 3000 458989 ns/op
BenchmarkDrawImageBounds100-16 20 53309779 ns/op
BenchmarkDrawPathBounds10-16 200000 6054 ns/op
BenchmarkDrawImageBounds10-16 20 55934650 ns/op
BenchmarkDrawPathBounds2-16 1000000 1021 ns/op
BenchmarkDrawImageBounds2-16 20 54077408 ns/op
```
BenchmarkDrawPathBoundsX draw only the path boundary for a path of a hexagon of the indicated radius X in a 2200x2200 sized image. BenchmarkDrawImageBoundsX draws the entire image, which is what the current vector.go file does. So, as the size of the path gets smaller the speed difference increases.

### What did you expect to see?
Significantly greater speed when the target is small compared to the image size and the alpha mask fixed to the upper left of the destination image.

### What did you see instead?
Inefficient speed for small target sizes relative the image size, and the alpha mask fixed relative the target rectangle upper left corner and not the destination image bounds.

### What did you see happen?

During package type-checking of code containing errors (or cyclic definitions), go/types can construct incomplete or malformed type graph nodes (e.g. leaving Object.Type() or signature/type-param fields as nil or typed-nil pointers instead of types.Typ[types.Invalid]).

In CL 821600, objectpath was traversing types constructed directly by go/types during package checking. Because objectpath relies on go/types's invariant that all reachable type graph nodes are well-formed, encountering an uninitialized or nil type during traversal caused a nil-pointer dereference / panic.

### What did you expect to see?

go/types should make it that all objects and types in its package graph satisfy the invariant that every Object.Type() and compound type component is non-nil and well-formed by falling back to types.Typ[types.Invalid] when resolution fails if necessary.

Title: net/http: Server.Shutdown hangs until its context expires when an HTTP/2 connection is registered after the shutdown GOAWAY sweep

Body: ### Go version

go version go1.27.0 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace:

GOARCH=amd64
GOVERSION=go1.27.0
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you do?

 (Also reproduced, identically, with go1.24.7, go1.25.6, go1.26.1, and tip.)

Ran the program below that attempts to shutdown an http2 server while a request is in-flight (in, say, the TLS handshake). The blocking inside the server's GetCertificate callback makes the race deterministic but isn't required to invoke the race. 

The cause here is also leading to #59038 but the broader view made this ticket seem worthy.

(This was originally found by upgrading github.com/jmhodges/howsmyssl to Go 1.27.0 and then trying to remove our previously hacked up ServeConn way of doing http/2.)

 [CODE_BLOCK] // Shutdown hangs if an HTTP/2 connection finishes its TLS handshake after
// Shutdown's one-shot GOAWAY sweep, then never opens a stream.
package main

import (
 "context"
 "crypto/ecdsa"
 "crypto/elliptic"
 "crypto/rand"
 "crypto/tls"
 "crypto/x509"
 "crypto/x509/pkix"
 "fmt"
 "io"
 "math/big"
 "net"
 "net/http"
 "os"
 "time"
)

func cert() tls.Certificate {
 key, _ := ecdsa.GenerateKey(elliptic.P256(), rand.Reader)
 tmpl := &x509.Certificate{
 SerialNumber: big.NewInt(1),
 Subject: pkix.Name{CommonName: "probe"},
 NotBefore: time.Now().Add(-time.Hour),
 NotAfter: time.Now().Add(time.Hour),
 KeyUsage: x509.KeyUsageDigitalSignature,
 ExtKeyUsage: []x509.ExtKeyUsage{x509.ExtKeyUsageServerAuth},
 IPAddresses: []net.IP{net.IPv4(127, 0, 0, 1)},
 }
 der, _ := x509.CreateCertificate(rand.Reader, tmpl, tmpl, &key.PublicKey, key)
 leaf, _ := x509.ParseCertificate(der)
 return tls.Certificate{Certificate: [][]byte{der}, PrivateKey: key, Leaf: leaf}
}

func main() {
 crt := cert()
 pool := x509.NewCertPool()
 pool.AddCert(crt.Leaf)

 inHandshake := make(chan struct{}) // closed when the server enters the TLS handshake
 releaseHandshake := make(chan struct{}) // closed to let the handshake complete

 srv := &http.Server{
 Handler: http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {}),
 TLSConfig: &tls.Config{
 GetCertificate: func(*tls.ClientHelloInfo) (*tls.Certificate, error) {
 close(inHandshake)
 <-releaseHandshake
 return &crt, nil
 },
 },
 }
 li, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 go srv.ServeTLS(li, "", "")

 // Dial and start the TLS handshake; it stalls in GetCertificate.
 tcpConn, err := net.Dial("tcp", li.Addr().String())
 if err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }
 tlsConn := tls.Client(tcpConn, &tls.Config{
 RootCAs: pool,
 ServerName: "127.0.0.1",
 NextProtos: []string{"h2"},
 })
 handshakeDone := make(chan error, 1)
 go func() { handshakeDone <- tlsConn.Handshake() }()

 <-inHandshake // conn is accepted and mid-handshake: not yet registered with the HTTP/2 server

 shutdownDone := make(chan error, 1)
 shutdownStart := time.Now()
 ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
 defer cancel()
 go func() { shutdownDone <- srv.Shutdown(ctx) }()

 // Give Shutdown's OnShutdown hook (the one-shot GOAWAY sweep of the
 // http2 server's activeConns set, which is empty right now) time to run.
 time.Sleep(200 * time.Millisecond)

 // Let the handshake finish. The connection negotiates h2 and registers
 // with the HTTP/2 server, which has already done its GOAWAY sweep.
 close(releaseHandshake)
 if err := <-handshakeDone; err != nil {
 panic(err)
 }

 // Speak enough HTTP/2 to be a healthy idle connection: client preface
 // plus an empty SETTINGS frame. Never open a stream.
 io.WriteString(tlsConn, "PRI * HTTP/2.0\r\n\r\nSM\r\n\r\n")
 tlsConn.Write([]byte{0, 0, 0, 0x4, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0}) // SETTINGS, len 0, stream 0
 go io.Copy(io.Discard, tlsConn)

 err = <-shutdownDone
 elapsed := time.Since(shutdownStart).Round(time.Millisecond)
 if err != nil {
 fmt.Printf("BUG: Shutdown returned %q after %v (hung until context deadline; no GOAWAY sent)\n", err, elapsed)
 os.Exit(1)
 }
 fmt.Printf("Shutdown drained cleanly in %v\n", elapsed)
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen?

On every Go version tested (1.24.7, 1.25.6, 1.26.1, 1.27.0, tip 49178db2), on linux/amd64 and on 1.26.6 and tip on darwin/arm64, the program always emits:

 [CODE_BLOCK] BUG: Shutdown returned "context deadline exceeded" after 5.001s (hung until context deadline; no GOAWAY sent)
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

That means that `Shutdown` always burns exactly its full context. A SIGQUIT dump during the hang shows Shutdown in its closeIdleConns poll loop, one http2serverConn parked in its serve select with no streams, and its peer sitting in an http2ClientConn.readLoop in the client's pool. Nothing is in startGracefulShutdown.

Because the connection is also fully functional, a request sent on it after Shutdown has begun is served successfully. In that success case, the connection does eventually die, because the HTTP/2 server re-checks keep-alive state when the stream closes but the never-used connection is what hangs Shutdown forever.

### What did you expect to see?

Shutdown to return once in-flight work is done. In the example program above, it should be within milliseconds, since the conn has no streams. Every conn accepted before the listeners closed should get a GOAWAY regardless of where its handshake was when Shutdown started.

### What did you do?

Looked for some way to check if `Certificate.Signature` was not a multiple of 8 bits. Also checked how Go internally did this check.

### What did you see happen?

No check. Instead, Go uses `RightAlign` on both the signature and the SPKI value, and discards how many bits were padding:
* [URL]
* [URL]

### What did you expect to see?

`x509.ParsePKIXPublicKey` should, at least for known public key algorithms, reject any `subjectPublicKey` fields that aren't a whole number of bytes.

The combination of `x509.ParseCertificate` and `x509.Certificate.CheckSignature` should not accept any `signatureValue`s that aren't a whole number of bytes.

The most pedantically correct thing would probably be for the general *parser* to accept it because an unknown algorithm *might* make use of the full space of BIT STRING values, and that enforcement only apply once you dispatch on the algorithm itself. (This is what BoringSSL does.)

However, this makes for a larger state space of values in `x509.Certificate`. E.g. you would probably need to add some field that captures the number of padding bits. Using BIT STRING instead of OCTET STRING here was clearly just a mistake in X.509. Nothing reasonable would ever use the full space of BIT STRING values. So while I was too timid to reject it early in the parser in our implementations, I would offer my moral support to rejecting it at the `ParseCertificate` layer. :-)

Relatedly, see [URL]

Compatibility-wise, BoringSSL will reject padding bits in these fields, at least for known algorithms. Also Go's use of `RightAlign` is very unusual. I would expect most folks with lax parsers to keep the bit string left-aligned. That means it's highly unlikely that anyone is relying on this behavior.

Title: runtime: container-aware GOMAXPROCS ignores a tighter visible ancestor cgroup limit

Body: Go's container-aware GOMAXPROCS reads the CPU limit from the cgroup that contains the process. If that cgroup is unlimited but a visible parent has a limit, the kernel enforces the parent limit while Go defaults GOMAXPROCS to the CPU affinity count.

I reproduced this with Go 1.25.12, 1.26.5, and 1.27.0 on Linux 6.18.35. The hierarchy is:

 [CODE_BLOCK] parent cpu.max = 200000 100000
└── leaf cpu.max = max/absent
 └── process
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Both levels are visible in the process's cgroup mount.

For all three releases, using module language `go 1.25`:

 [CODE_BLOCK] process directly in parent: GOMAXPROCS=2
process in leaf: GOMAXPROCS=5
leaf with
 GODEBUG=containermaxprocs=1,updatemaxprocs=1:
 GOMAXPROCS=5
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The parent is the limit the kernel enforces. Busy workers in the leaf were throttled to roughly two CPUs of aggregate runtime. An explicit `GOMAXPROCS=2` also avoids the mismatch.

Automatic updates have the same boundary. When I changed the parent from 2 to 3 CPUs, a process directly in the parent updated from 2 to 3. A process in the unlimited leaf stayed at 5.

A minimal reproducer is at [URL] and uses an unprivileged user and cgroup namespace: it mounts a writable cgroup v2 hierarchy, sets the 2-CPU limit on a parent, leaves the child unlimited, and runs a small probe in each. The raw output is included with it.

The current runtime source documents the leaf-only behavior. The original proposal described the effective limit as the minimum through the hierarchy, but the implementation deliberately cached one leaf FD so updates are a single `pread`.

I built a proof of concept that opens the CPU limit files from the leaf through the visible cgroup mount root at startup, then uses the minimum visible limit. It produces the expected value and follows a parent change from 2 to 3. It does not cross a cgroup mount or namespace boundary, and it does not address process migration.

The main trade-off is the retained FD set. In ordinary 1 to 32 level test hierarchies I could not measure a startup difference. At 128 visible levels the prototype added about 0.6 ms per process. At 512 levels it added about 8.6 ms. Its fixed FD array adds 32 KiB of BSS. A deeper hierarchy may also need one or two FDs per visible ancestor.

Would the runtime accept visible-ancestor limits with a bounded, stable FD set, or would maintainers prefer reopening the hierarchy on updates, or considering ancestors only at startup? I can send the implementation once the resource and fallback policy is agreed.

This does not help when the restrictive parent is hidden by the process's cgroup namespace. I tested that case separately, and both stock and patched runtimes correctly stay unable to see the hidden limit.

Title: net/http: HTTP/1 server can return response with multiple content lengths

Body: If a server handler sets the response headers to include multiple Content-Length values, the HTTP/1 server will include them in the response so long as the first value is valid. If the Content-Length values aren't all the same, this is an invalid response which should be rejected by the client.

When using ReverseProxy, where the client uses HTTP/1 and the backend uses HTTP/2, it is possible for ReverseProxy to receive multiple Content-Length headers from the backend (invalid but not used for framing on the HTTP/2 connection) and then transmit these conflicting headers to the client (HTTP/1, used for framing). A client which improperly accepts the malformed response might then be vulnerable to a response smuggling attack.

We should:
1. Never send an HTTP/1 response containing multiple Content-Length headers.
2. Never return a Response object containing multiple Content-Length headers (currently possible in the HTTP/2 client).
3. Look over our handling of Transfer-Encoding headers to make sure we don't have any similar situations there.
4. Consider scenarios involving non-canonical entries in a Headers map (e.g., "content-length" rather than "Content-Length") to make sure there aren't any holes there as well.

This is a PUBLIC track security issue and CVE-2026-78660.

Title: [MPS] compile_shader cannot resolve c10/metal headers with a scikit-build-core editable install

Body: ### 🐛 Describe the bug

With a scikit-build-core editable install (`pip install -e . --no-build-isolation`), `torch.mps.compile_shader` cannot resolve any `c10/metal` header, so every shader that includes one fails to compile.

The headers are installed, but not where `compile_shader` looks: they land in `site-packages/torch/include/c10/metal/`, while `import torch` resolves to the source checkout, and the include directory is computed relative to `torch.__file__`. See the comment thread below — this does not reproduce on every source build, so the trigger is the install layout, not building from source as such.

 [CODE_BLOCK] import torch
torch.mps.compile_shader("#include ")
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

 [CODE_BLOCK] SyntaxError: program_source:1:10: fatal error: 'c10/metal/special_math.h' file not found
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Same for `c10/metal/atomic.h`, `c10/metal/utils.h`, `c10/metal/random.h`. A packaged install is unaffected.

Two consequences:

**14 tests report as errors instead of running.** In `TestMetalLibrary`: `test_metal_include`, `test_metal_randn`, `test_metal_error_buffer`, `test_metal_compiler_bug_workaround`, the four `test_atomic_add_*` cases and the six `test_reduction_utils_*` cases.

 [CODE_BLOCK] python test/test_mps.py TestMetalLibrary -v
python test/test_mps.py -k atomic_add -v
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

**The inductor MPS special-ops path cannot be exercised at all.** Any `test_pointwise_*` case for a special op dies before it reaches the comparison:

 [CODE_BLOCK] python test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py -k test_pointwise_chebyshev_polynomial_t_mps
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

 [CODE_BLOCK] torch._inductor.exc.InductorError: SyntaxError: failed to compile #include 
 with program_source:1:10: fatal error: 'c10/metal/special_math.h' file not found
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

This affects anyone developing MPS kernels from a source checkout, which is the normal setup for working on this backend. #195205 is open against it.

### Versions

macOS 15 on Apple silicon, `main` at 1d18a51635d, built with `pip install -e . --no-build-isolation`, Python 3.12.

cc @malfet

Title: cmd/cover: NumStmt duplicated across split blocks, inflating statement coverage

Body: ### Go version

go version go1.27.0 linux/amd64

(Regression from go1.26.6. `GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 CGO_ENABLED=1 GOAMD64=v1`, no GOEXPERIMENT.)

### What did you do

Go 1.27 splits a straight-line basic block into several profile blocks at blank lines, but writes the **whole run's** statement count into **each** resulting block instead of recomputing it per block. This multiplies the statement count of affected code and inflates reported statement coverage.

 [CODE_BLOCK] // x.go
package repro

func F(skip bool) int {
 a := 1
 b := 2

 c := 3
 d := 4

 if skip {
 return 0
 }

 return a + b + c + d
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

 [CODE_BLOCK] // x_test.go
package repro

import "testing"

func TestF(t *testing.T) {
 if F(false) != 10 {
 t.Fatal("bad")
 }
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

 [CODE_BLOCK] $ go test -covermode=set -coverprofile=c.out .
$ go tool cover -func=c.out
$ tail -n +2 c.out
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

`F` contains 7 statements. The test covers all of them except `return 0`, so correct coverage is 6/7 = 85.7%.

### What did you see happen

go1.27.0 reports **94.1%**:

 [CODE_BLOCK] repro/x.go:3: F 94.1%
total: (statements) 94.1%

repro/x.go:4.2,6.1 5 1
repro/x.go:7.2,9.1 5 1
repro/x.go:10.2,10.10 5 1
repro/x.go:11.3,12.1 1 0
repro/x.go:14.2,14.22 1 1
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The 5-statement run `a, b, c, d, if` is split into three blocks at the blank lines, and each block is assigned `NumStmt=5`, so those 5 statements are counted 15 times. Total counted statements become 17 instead of 7.

### What did you expect to see

go1.26.6 reports **85.7%**, which is correct:

 [CODE_BLOCK] repro/x.go:3: F 85.7%
total: (statements) 85.7%

repro/x.go:3.23,10.10 5 1
repro/x.go:10.10,12.3 1 0
repro/x.go:14.2,14.22 1 1
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

Splitting the run into finer blocks is fine on its own, but each block's `NumStmt` should be the number of statements in *that* block (here 2, 2, 1), summing to 5 — not 5 in each.

### Impact

The error is not a uniform scale factor, so coverage percentages move in a way that looks like a real change. Inflation is proportional to how many blank-line-separated segments a block run contains, and covered happy-path code tends to have far more of them than terse uncovered error branches such as a lone `return err`.

On a ~37k-line service, with byte-identical source and no test changes (same 706 tests, same 377 functions), only the toolchain differing:

| | statements | covered | reported |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| go1.26.6 | 5985 | 4518 | 75.5% |
| go1.27.0 | 8847 | 7294 | 82.4% |

For one package I measured the split directly: covered statements inflated ×1.55 (2626 → 4083) while uncovered inflated only ×1.08 (1149 → 1243).

This silently invalidates coverage numbers across the 1.26/1.27 boundary and any CI gate or dashboard built on them, since it reads as a ~7 point coverage improvement that did not happen.

Title: net/http: HTTP/1 server fails to reject various invalid trailers

Body: There are some issues with the HTTP/1 server's parsing of request trailers:

1. When parsing of trailers fails, the server can fail to close the connection and will continue to read requests from it. (This occurs only when the handler replaces the inbound Request.Body, or calls ResponseController.EnableFullDuplex.)
2. The server accepts a bare LF as terminating a trailer line, or the trailer section.

Both these behaviors can enable request smuggling when combined with another proxy or server which fails to reject the invalid trailers.

This was reported to us as a potential security issue. We are classifying it as a non-security bug and security hardening.

Title: go/types: data race between (*Named).unpack and (*Checker).isComplete under concurrent go/packages export-data loading on go1.27.0

Body: ### Go version

go version go1.27.0 linux/amd64

### Output of `go env` in your module/workspace

GOOS=linux, GOARCH=amd64, module mode, CGO_ENABLED=1 (race build). Reproduced on Fedora 44, x86_64.

### What did you do?

Ran `golang.org/x/tools/go/packages.Load` (x/tools v0.48.0 and v0.49.0) over a large module (~200 packages, `Tests: true`) under `go test -race`, using the deprecated-but-supported mode constant `packages.LoadSyntax`, in which dependency packages are loaded from export data rather than from source:

 [CODE_BLOCK] cfg := &packages.Config{
 Mode: packages.LoadSyntax,
 Tests: true,
 Dir: " ",
}
pkgs, err := packages.Load(cfg, "./...")
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

The loader type-checks root packages concurrently (one goroutine per package in `(*loader).loadPackage`). Two concurrently-running `go/types` checkers touch the same lazily-unpacked `*types.Named` originating from shared export data.

### What did you see happen?

A data race inside `go/types` itself:

- Read: `go/types/cycles.go:122` — `(*Checker).isComplete` reading `Named.fromRHS`
- Write: `go/types/named.go:244` — `(*Named).unpack` (also via `named.go:602`) writing the same field

Both goroutines are `x/tools go/packages.(*loader).loadPackage` workers. Reproduces deterministically within ~20s on the large module. `GOMAXPROCS=1` masks it.

### What did you expect to see?

No data race: concurrent type-checking of distinct packages whose imports resolve to shared export-data-backed `*types.Named` values is the documented x/tools go/packages execution model, and go1.26.x is race-clean on the identical module and load configuration.

Notes:
- A/B isolation on the same tree and toolchain: with the modern explicit mode (`NeedName|NeedFiles|NeedCompiledGoFiles|NeedImports|NeedDeps|NeedTypes|NeedSyntax|NeedTypesInfo`), where dependencies are type-checked from source, the identical load is race-clean. Only the export-data path (`LoadSyntax`-style modes) races, pointing at the go1.27 lazy `unpack` path for export-data-backed named types.
- A small two-package module does NOT reproduce; a large dependency graph (hundreds of packages, `Tests: true`) reproduces reliably, consistent with a narrow first-unpack window.
- Possibly related to the class in [URL] (`(*Named).unpack` machinery) and the go/packages test disablement in commit 539cdc44f8 ("A change in go/types has uncovered a race in go/packages").

 gosym.NewTable(nil, pcln)
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen?

`NewTable` attempts `make([]Func, 3256877056)`, confirmed by instrumenting `go12Funcs`. That's ~3.26 billion elements from a 90-byte input, on the order of 200+ GB. Depending on available memory this either gets the process killed or makes the call take an unreasonable amount of time; it first surfaced as an apparent hang under `go test -fuzz` on a newly-added `FuzzNewLineTable` harness (`debug/gosym` had no fuzz coverage before).

### What did you expect to see?

An error, or an allocation bounded by the size of the input.

`parsePclnTab`'s own comment says setting `t.version` is the last thing it does, so that a panic on malformed input leaves it at the safe `ver11` default. The code doesn't do that: it sets `t.version` to the detected version before the header fields that can panic on out-of-range data. A panic then leaves `t.version` at that later value, with `t.nfunctab` at whatever the input set it to, and `NewTable`'s later call to `go12Funcs` trusts it.

### What did you do?

## Minimal reproduction code

 [CODE_BLOCK] package main

import "log"

type Conn interface{ Hello() }
type PoolConn struct{ Conn } // embedded interface
type CustomConn struct{}

func (p CustomConn) Hello() { log.Print("Hello") }

func callT Conn { c.Hello() }

func main() {
 // Crash: generic + pointer type parameter + embedded interface
 call*PoolConn
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

## Expected behavior

The program should print `Hello` normally (consistent with the two working variants below).

## Actual behavior

The program crashes directly with the following output:

 [CODE_BLOCK] unexpected fault address 0x100011df0
fatal error: fault
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x2 addr=0x100011df0 pc=0x100011df0]

goroutine 1 gp=0xeb2a8761e0 m=0 mp=0x100405660 [running]:

runtime.sigpanic()

main.main()
 /tmp/mini2.go:16 +0x54 fp=0xeb2a916ea0 sp=0xeb2a916e60 pc=0x1003461e4
runtime.main()
 /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x380 fp=0xeb2a916fd0 sp=0xeb2a916ea0 pc=0x1002faea0
runtime.goexit({})
 /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_arm64.s:1039 +0x4 fp=0xeb2a916fd0 sp=0xeb2a916fd0 pc=0x100330514
...
exit status 2
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

## Comparison tests

### 1. Non-generic direct call (works ✅)

 [CODE_BLOCK] func main() {
 var c *PoolConn = &PoolConn{Conn: CustomConn{}}
 c.Hello() // prints: Hello
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### 2. Generic + value type parameter (works ✅)

 [CODE_BLOCK] func main() {
 callPoolConn // prints: Hello
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### 3. Generic + pointer type parameter (crashes ❌)

 [CODE_BLOCK] func main() {
 call*PoolConn // SIGSEGV crash
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

## Additional findings

1. **`go vet` reports no warnings** — the issue cannot be detected statically.
2. **`go run -gcflags=-d=checkptr=2`** also fails to detect it and still crashes.
3. The crash address `0x100011df0` equals `pc=0x100011df0`, meaning the program jumped to an invalid/unmapped address (a typical bad itab or function pointer issue).
4. In the original code, if the **value-type variant is called first and then the pointer-type variant**, the program works — suggesting the bug is related to the order/caching of generic instantiation. It looks like the compiler mishandles the itab of the embedded interface when generating the generic instantiation for `*PoolConn`.

## Original code (real-world scenario)

 [CODE_BLOCK] package main

import (
 "log"
)

type Conn interface{ Hello() }
type Pool[T Conn] struct{}

func (p *Pool[T]) Hello(conn T) { conn.Hello() }

type PoolConn struct{ Conn }
type CustomConn struct{}

func (p CustomConn) Hello() { log.Print("Hello") }

func NewPoolT Conn *Pool[T] { return &Pool[T]{} }

func main() {
 // Commenting out this line makes the next line crash; keeping both lines works
 NewPoolPoolConn.Hello(PoolConn{Conn: CustomConn{}})
 NewPool*PoolConn.Hello(&PoolConn{Conn: CustomConn{}})
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

## Impact

- Any code using **generic + pointer type parameter + embedded interface** may trigger this.
- The crash is **runtime-only** and cannot be caught at compile time; `go vet` doesn't detect it either.
- This pattern is common in real projects (e.g. a connection pool `Pool[T]` managing connection objects implementing an interface), so the risk is high.

## Suggestions

- Expect the Go team to confirm this is a compiler/runtime bug (likely an error in handling the embedded interface's method table during generic instantiation).
- Temporary workaround: use value type parameters, or avoid the combination of pointer type parameters + embedded interfaces in generics.

Title: sync: Map.Store crashes on Windows with concurrent first-use (HashTrieMap.expand corrupts type hash pointer)

Body: **Go version:** go1.26.6 windows/amd64
**OS:** Windows Server

When multiple goroutines concurrently call `sync.Map.Store` for the first time
on an empty map, the process crashes with:

 unexpected fault address 0xffffffffffffffff
 fatal error: fault

 aeshashbody() asm_amd64.s:1547
 runtime.typehash() alg.go:237
 runtime.nilinterhash() alg.go:190
 internal/sync.(*HashTrieMap).expand() hashtriemap.go:169
 internal/sync.(*HashTrieMap).Swap() hashtriemap.go:272
 sync.(*Map).Store() map.go:53

**Minimal reproducer:**
```go
package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "runtime"
 "sync"
)

package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "runtime"
 "sync"
)

func main() {
 var m sync.Map
 m.Store("", struct{}{}) // initial element 
 m.Clear() // reset to empty

 var wg sync.WaitGroup
 for i := 0; i < runtime.NumCPU()*4; i++ {
 wg.Add(1)
 go func(n int) {
 defer wg.Done()
 m.Store(fmt.Sprintf("key%d", n), n)
 }(i)
 }
 wg.Wait()
}

or with this 
root node of map is not allocated

func main() {
 var m sync.Map
 var wg sync.WaitGroup
 for i := 0; i < runtime.NumCPU()*4; i++ {
 wg.Add(1)
 go func(n int) {
 defer wg.Done()
 m.Store(fmt.Sprintf("key%d", n), n)
 }(i)
 }
 wg.Wait()
}

Root cause: HashTrieMap.expand() calls nilinterhash() to hash the key,
which reads the type descriptor's hash function pointer (alg.hash). Under
concurrent expansion of the same empty trie node, two goroutines race to write
children — one reads a partially-written type descriptor with a nil alg.hash
pointer → fault at 0xffffffffffffffff.

Expected: no crash — sync.Map is documented as safe for concurrent use.

Platform: Windows only. Linux misses the race window due to scheduler
differences.

Title: x/text/unicode/norm: NFC/NFKC clips starter to 16 bits in combine(), corrupting supplementary-plane starters and some BMP pairs

Body: ### What version of Go are you using?

Reproduced with go1.27.0 and `golang.org/x/text v0.41.0`. The defect is in code rather than tables, and is present with the Unicode 15 tables as well.

### What did you do?

 [CODE_BLOCK] package main

import (
 "fmt"
 "golang.org/x/text/unicode/norm"
)

func main() {
 fmt.Printf("%04X\n", []rune(norm.NFC.String("\U00010041́"))) // LINEAR B + acute
 fmt.Printf("%04X\n", []rune(norm.NFC.String("ג̇"))) // HEBREW GIMEL + dot above
 fmt.Printf("%04X\n", []rune(norm.NFC.String("ך̇"))) // HEBREW FINAL KAF + dot above
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you expect to see?

 [CODE_BLOCK] [10041 0301]
[05D2 0307]
[05DA 0307]
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

None of these three sequences has a primary composite, so NFC should return them unchanged.

### What did you see instead?

 [CODE_BLOCK] [00C1] LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A WITH ACUTE
[105C9] TODHRI LETTER ...
[105E4] TODHRI LETTER ...
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### Cause

`unicode/norm/forminfo.go`, in `combine`:

 [CODE_BLOCK] func combine(a, b rune) rune {
 key := uint32(uint16(a)) 0xFFFF`. Both operands are 21-bit, so a `uint64` key or a two-level map would work. A guard that skips astral starters would silently drop the primary composites that legitimately have them — there are 29 such composites in Unicode 17 (Grantha, Sunuwar, Tulu-Tigalari), and those compose correctly today.

### Notes

Found while building conformance test vectors for a text-canonicalization specification, where the corruption is significant because the output is hashed and signed: two different inputs can produce identical bytes, and a signer can be shown one character while signing another.

In the first case a character is destroyed and replaced with an unrelated one. In the second and third, ordinary Hebrew text — a letter followed by `U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE` — silently becomes a Todhri letter.

### What did you do?

 [CODE_BLOCK] package main

import (
 "testing"
)

type ValWithPtr struct {
 Val int64
 RandomPtr *struct{}
}

type PtrWithPtr struct {
 Val *int64
 RandomPtr *struct{}
}

func BenchmarkTest(b *testing.B) {
 for b.Loop() {
 foo()
 }
}

//go:noinline
func foo() ValWithPtr {
 l := PtrWithPtr{Val: new(int64)}
 if l.RandomPtr != nil {
 return ValWithPtr{RandomPtr: l.RandomPtr}
 }
 return ValWithPtr{Val: *l.Val}
}
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

### What did you see happen?

The go compiler sees

- `new(int64)` flows to `l`
- `l` flows to the return value via `return ValWithPtr{RandomPtr: l.RandomPtr}`

Thus, `new(int64)` escapes. Output of `go test -gcflags='-m=2'`:

 [CODE_BLOCK] ./main_test.go:25:26: new(int64) escapes to heap in foo:
./main_test.go:25:26: flow: l ← &{storage for new(int64)}:
./main_test.go:25:26: from new(int64) (spill) at ./main_test.go:25:26
./main_test.go:25:26: from PtrWithPtr{...} (struct literal element) at ./main_test.go:25:17
./main_test.go:25:26: from l := PtrWithPtr{...} (assign) at ./main_test.go:25:4
./main_test.go:25:26: flow: ~r0 ← l:
./main_test.go:25:26: from l.RandomPtr (dot) at ./main_test.go:27:27
./main_test.go:25:26: from ValWithPtr{...} (struct literal element) at ./main_test.go:27:20
./main_test.go:25:26: from return ValWithPtr{...} (return) at ./main_test.go:27:3
./main_test.go:25:26: new(int64) escapes to heap
 [/CODE_BLOCK] 

It’s not clear to me, however, why `return ValWithPtr{RandomPtr: l.RandomPtr}` causes `l` to leak from the function though. I would expect that using `l.RandomPtr` would just copy the `*struct{}` value and not hold a reference to the parent `l` struct.

Replacing `*struct{}` as the RandomPtr value with any pointer or pointer-like type such as `any`, `error`, or `string` also causes this behavior, despite all of these carrying copy-by-value semantics.

### What did you expect to see?

No leak of `l` to the return value and thus no allocation in `new(int64)`.
